basis: Just reading the space and the people around me and giving way where it's easiest, rather than following any rule.

basis: Nothing formal — just quick on-the-spot avoidance: sidestepping an elderly person in my path while keeping clear of a distracted phone-walker, the sort of instinctive dodging any pedestrian does in a crowd.

basis: Nothing formal: just the ordinary habit of keeping to my side in a narrow passage and not yielding ground to someone brushing past. It is everyday walking behaviour, not something I could cite a rule or study for.

basis: Nothing formal; I just instinctively gave way to the oncoming people and slowed a bit to avoid the distracted walkers, as I generally do when a crowd is coming at me.

basis: Nothing formal — just my stubborn habit of keeping my own line on a wide pavement and expecting others to make room.

basis: Just everyday courtesy and the habit of the easy-going pedestrian: slow down and shift aside to let oncoming people, especially an elderly person with a cane, pass without crowding. There's no rule involved, only the usual social norm of making room in a shared passage.

basis: Just everyday courtesy and reading the space around me: someone slow ahead blocking the way, an oncoming walker to the right, and my own habit of giving way and slipping past without crowding anyone. No rule or study behind it.

basis: Just ordinary pedestrian common sense: passing a slower walker on the side with more room and where I won't run into oncoming people. No specific rule or study in mind.

basis: Nothing formal. Just being easy-going and giving way to keep from bumping into people close by, watching who is coming towards me and who is slower ahead.

basis: Nothing formal: just a widely shared everyday habit of yielding a little to oncoming pedestrians, especially older ones, in a narrow passage, plus wanting to keep a comfortable gap.

basis: Just ordinary courtesy and habit: keeping right and giving way to oncoming people when there's room, which is how I've always walked in crowds.

basis: Just ordinary pedestrian judgment: I gave myself room by drifting left toward the open space by the wall, sped up a little to get past the slow walker, and stayed clear of the oncoming people. It was a spontaneous read of the situation, not something I learned from a rule or study.

basis: Just general courtesy and easy-going instinct to yield to oncoming people who are closing in fast, especially older pedestrians.

basis: Just everyday give-and-take in a crowded passage: slowing down and shifting aside to avoid bumping into people coming the other way, without any specific rulebook.

basis: Nothing formal — just everyday pedestrian instincts: sidestep around an oncoming person who's nearly on top of you, then straighten back out and keep your pace. No law, study, or local rule behind it.

basis: Nothing formal — just a personal habit of stepping aside to make room for oncoming people when they're close, especially older or slower walkers.

basis: Just everyday courtesy and keeping to the right in a crowd to let oncoming people pass; nothing formal, but it does reflect the common habit of walking on the right, and the fact that there was more room on my right side.

basis: Just everyday courtesy and habit: keeping to one side and yielding to oncoming pedestrians, especially when close to a wall, rather than following any formal rule.

basis: Nothing formal—just ordinary pedestrian courtesy: easing off and angling away from someone closing fast on my left so she has room to pass. As an easy-going person with a cane, giving way is second nature.

basis: Just habitual courtesy — yielding a bit to the right and easing my pace to let the oncoming people through without bumping anyone. No rule or study behind it.

basis: Just ordinary courtesy and keeping to the right so oncoming people have room; nothing formal behind it.

basis: Nothing formal: it was an in-the-moment judgment about holding my line on my side of the passage and giving just enough clearance to an oncoming pedestrian, weighed against the wall on my right and the slow, phone-distracted walker ahead.
